newsitem.title: USA: Variety is spice of life when it comes to food tastes.
newsitem.headline: Variety is spice of life when it comes to food tastes.

text.p: Thanks to an increasingly eclectic American palate, sales of tortillas have flattened sales of bagels, while Afghan flatbread and Ethiopian injera have taken a bite out of croissant consumption, according to the USA Weekend magazine that will be available Sunday.

The Nov. 8 issue of the magazine, featuring the top 25 food trends of 1996, said sales of tortillas rose to $2.5 billion last year compared with $300 million in 1980, according to the Tortilla Industry Association in Encino, Calif. Tortillas contain about 115 calories each.
Sales of muffins, croissants and bagels, meanwhile, represent only 9.6 percent of supermarket bakery sales.
But the trend toward low-calorie, low-fat breads may have more to do with taste than health.

The article notes that only 35 percent of Americans are doing all they can to eat a balanced diet, down from 44 percent in 1991. A lack of time and a reluctance to forego favourite foods are the biggest obstacles to eating well.

Processed and ready-to-eat choices such as soups, soft drinks, and juices remain staples in the American diet. Consumption of non-citrus fruit juices by children more than tripled between 1977 and 1994, sweetened by the popular kid-sized juice cartons.
And each year, Americans buy 2.4 billion cans of soup, enough to circle the equator six times.
